slot.brief: For a simple one-electron or two-electron half-cell (e.g. metal ion concentration given at 298 K), compute the electrode potential using the Nernst equation; straightforward plug-in.

stem: At $298\ \text{K}$, a hydrogen electrode has pH $2$ and hydrogen pressure $1\ \text{bar}$. Find its reduction potential. Take $E^\circ=0\ \text{V}$ and $2.303RT/F=0.059\ \text{V}$.
working:
$2\text{H}^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2$; $n=2$.
$E=E^\circ-\dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{P_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^+]^2}\right)$
$pH=2 \Rightarrow [\text{H}^+]=10^{-2}$; $P_{\text{H}_2}=1$.
$E=-\dfrac{0.059}{2}\log(10^4)=-0.118\ \text{V}$

Independent check: For $2H^+ + 2e^- \to H_2$, $E=-(0.059/2)\log\!\left(p_{H_2}/[H^+]^2\right)$. With $p_{H_2}=1$ bar and $[H^+]=10^{-2}$, $E=-0.118\,\text{V}$.
solution:
For $2\mathrm{H}^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2$, the Nernst equation is
$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.059}{2}\log\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{[\mathrm{H}^+]^2}\right).$$
Using $P_{\mathrm{H}_2}=1$ bar and $[\mathrm{H}^+]=10^{-2}$, $E=-\frac{0.059}{2}\log(10^4)=-0.118\ \text{V}$.
